title: What a Throw Does on the Way Out: Catching by Reference, Rethrowing, and the Destructors That Run

questions.question: A function throws std::invalid_argument("bad value 12abc") and the caller writes catch (std::exception e). What does e.what() give?
options: std::exception: the derived part and its message are cut off by catching by value
questions.explanation: Caught by reference it gave the specific message.

questions.question: What is the right way to write a handler for a specific exception?
options: By const reference, most specific handler first

questions.question: What is the difference between throw e; and throw; inside a handler?
options: throw e; throws a copy made from the declared type of e, throw; rethrows the very object with its own type
questions.explanation: throw e; gave cut down to exception, throw; gave still invalid_argument.

questions.question: What does parse_all do before rethrowing?
options: It records which item failed, then uses a bare throw; so the caller still sees the original type
questions.explanation: The caller learns both where and what.

questions.question: Three guards A, B, C are alive when a throw happens. In what order do things happen?
options: handler, then drop A, B, C
drop C, drop B, drop A, then the handler: reverse order of construction, before the handler starts
drop A, B, C, then the handler
questions.explanation: That is why cleanup belongs in a destructor.

questions.question: A function releases a motor on the line after a call that can throw. What happens when it throws?
options: The release is skipped, since a throw leaves at once and only destructors run on the way out
questions.explanation: Put the release in a destructor so the unwinding does it.
